english:
The discriminative faculty, though covered, continues to reveal to man the misery and defects in worldly enjoyments and possessions from time to time. But because man does not give importance to it, he remains entangled in worldly enjoyments and possessions. Therefore, man should give importance to this discriminative faculty and make it permanent. He has complete freedom to do so. By making the discriminative faculty permanent, he can completely eradicate the defects of passion, anger, and other vices. That is why Lord Krishna cautions man with the word 'ih' (in this world) that he has a rare opportunity now to conquer passion and anger and become happy forever.

The human body has been obtained only for the purpose of liberation. Therefore, every human being is capable, entitled, and strong enough to bear the force of passion and anger. In this matter, there is no consideration of caste, stage of life, etc.

Since death is unpredictable and can occur at any moment, one should first learn to bear the force of passion and anger. One should not be controlled by passion and anger - this caution should be exercised throughout life. This task can be accomplished by man himself, and no one else can do it for him. The opportunity to do this task is available only in the human body, not in other bodies. Therefore, this task should be done before the body is lost - this is the idea conveyed in these verses.

From the above verses, another idea can be derived that one should learn to bear the force of passion and anger before the body starts acting under their influence. The reason is that once the body starts acting according to passion and anger, the body and the senses are no longer under one's control. The desire to possess worldly objects arises first, followed by the determination to acquire them. As soon as this determination arises, one should become cautious, thinking, "I am a seeker, I should not get entangled in worldly objects; this is not the task of a seeker." In this way, as soon as the determination arises, one should give it up.

Due to attachment to worldly objects, determinations such as "such and such objects are beautiful and pleasurable" arise. After the determination arises, the desire to acquire those objects is born, and anger arises towards those who hinder their acquisition.

The meaning of bearing the force of passion and anger is to prevent them from arising in the first place. After the determination of passion and anger arises, the force comes, and after the force comes, it becomes difficult to control passion and anger. Therefore, the idea of the above verses seems to be to prevent the determination of passion and anger from arising. The reason is that when the determination of passion and anger arises, the mind becomes disturbed, agitated, and conflicted, and man cannot be considered happy in such a state. However, in this verse, the person who bears the force of passion and anger is called 'sukhī' (happy). Another point is that man can control the force of passion and anger out of fear of a powerful person or out of greed for wealth. However, controlling the force of passion and anger in this way does not make him happy, because he becomes entangled in fear and greed, just as he was earlier entangled in passion and anger.

In this verse, the person who bears the force of passion and anger is called a 'yogī' (yuktaḥ), but without giving up determinations, one cannot become a yogī (as stated in the second verse of the sixth chapter of the Gītā). Therefore, although controlling the force of passion and anger is good, it is more appropriate for a seeker to prevent their determinations from arising.

The method to prevent the determinations of passion and anger is to not consider them as one's own. The reason is that we (the self) are permanent, while passion and anger are transient. Therefore, they are not our companions. Another point is that we know passion and anger as separate from ourselves. The object that we know as separate from ourselves is not within us. A third point is that it is possible to become free from passion and anger - 'kāma-krodha-viyuktānām' (Gītā 5.26), 'etair vimuktaḥ' (Gītā 16.22). One can become free from them only if one is already free from them in reality. A fourth point is that Lord Krishna has stated that passion and anger (which are the gross forms of attachment and aversion) are the defects of nature (prakṛti) (Gītā 13.6). Therefore, they exist in nature, not in ourselves, because our true nature is unchanging. This proves that passion and anger are not within us.

The verse is: 
sa sukhi 

Word-by-word breakdown: 
sa: he, that person
sukhi: happy 

The verse can be translated as: 
He (that person) is happy. 

Another verse is: 
yuktaḥ 

Word-by-word breakdown: 
yuktaḥ: united, a yogi 

The verse can be translated as: 
(a yogi, or) united. 

Another verse is: 
kāma-krodha-viyuktānām 

Word-by-word breakdown: 
kāma: passion, desire
krodha: anger
viyuktānām: of those who are free from 

The verse can be translated as: 
of those who are free from passion and anger. 

Another verse is: 
etair vimuktaḥ 

Word-by-word breakdown: 
etair: from these (passion and anger)
vimuktaḥ: liberated 

The verse can be translated as: 
liberated from these (passion and anger).
